Triggers.value: Talk about people loosing loved ones

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Going to or near the place where the event happened
Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Being emotionally close or intimate with others

Memory.value: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words.
I know what happened but I am unable to find words to describe it
There are parts of the event that I simply cannot remember no matter how hard I try

I can't stop bad things from happening to me

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Intrinsic Fault: There is something about me that made the event happen
issues.explanation: The appraisal that something about the patient made the event happen is difficult to reconcile with terrorism trauma, which is typically externally caused and indiscriminate. Self-blame can occur, but this specific intrinsic-causation item is not well supported by the rest of the profile and is clinically hard to explain here.

vignette:
Carmen is a 78-year-old Latina widow who works from home as a call center agent-a job she took after retiring from community organizing, believing the distance from public spaces would keep her safe. Ten years ago, she and her husband were volunteering at a neighborhood festival when a bomb hidden in a flower planter detonated near the stage. The blast sent debris slicing through the crowd; a metal shard lodged in her neck, fracturing a vertebra, and in the chaos she saw her husband fall, then never get up. In the months that followed, she could not tell anyone what had happened-she knew the facts, but when she opened her mouth to speak the words felt like gravel, and she would fall silent. Whole minutes of that afternoon remained blank, as if erased, and she learned to stop trying to fill them. The neck pain, a constant ache radiating down her left shoulder, became the only story her body would tell.

The anniversaries of the bombing terrify her. As each September nears, Carmen feels a tightening in her throat and begins scanning news articles for mentions of the date; she arranges to take those days off from work, turning down phone shifts so no caller can bring up loss or grief. Even a casual remark from a customer about losing a family member-common in the support calls she handles-makes her hand tremble as she reaches for the mute button, and she will disconnect as soon as decorum allows. Talking about the event itself is worse: once a new colleague asked about her scar, and Carmen answered in monosyllables, then avoided that colleague's calls for weeks afterward. She also avoids the neighborhood where the festival was held, taking a longer bus route even though it makes her late, because the sight of the community hall-now rebuilt and painted a cheerful yellow-fills her with a shame she cannot name.

Her memory of the event is fragmented, non-verbal, lodged in sensations rather than story. She can still feel the heat of the blast and the ringing in her ears, but she cannot connect that sensation to a coherent timeline. When a trigger-say, a customer's story about a lost spouse-brings the event to mind, she experiences the same wordlessness: the more she tries to put it into language, the more the gaps seem to widen, and she ends up staring at her computer screen, mouth dry, having forgotten what the customer just said. After the memory had surfaced in this way, even the most ordinary sounds-a kettle whistling, a door slamming-felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore. That failure to speak, to remember, feeds a deepening sense of hopelessness: she believes she has already failed in her most important role-protecting her husband, keeping their family intact-and now she cannot even tell her own story. Each triggered memory confirms that she is powerless, that bad things will keep happening and she will never be able to stop them or even describe them.

Avoiding the location, anniversaries, and intimacy does not bring relief. Instead, it leaves her more isolated, with fewer people around to remind her of the details she has lost, so the memory stays locked in that same fragmented, wordless state. And the longer she avoids, the more she interprets her avoidance as proof that she cannot cope, that she is too weak to face the past-another way she has failed. The hopelessness has grown so heavy that she rarely thinks about the future; when she does, she sees only a flat continuation of this present, with no possibility of change.

What finally brought Carmen to seek help was a call from a stranger whose voice, soft and elderly, reminded her of her husband's. She froze, could not speak, and the caller hung up. That night, she woke with the neck pain worse than ever, and for the first time she admitted to herself that she could not go on this way-afraid of dates, of conversations, of everyone who might ask her to remember. She is not sure therapy can undo what happened, but she is terrified of living another year as a woman who cannot find the words for her own life.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not convey that the traumatic memory itself leads to or activates triggers; instead, triggers (e.g., anniversaries, customer stories) bring the memory to mind, but the reverse causal relationship is absent.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Memory → Triggers: The vignette does not convey that the traumatic memory itself leads to or activates triggers; instead, triggers (e.g., anniversaries, customer stories) bring the memory to mind, but the reverse causal relationship is absent.
  e.g. "After the memory had surfaced, even the most ordinary things — a kettle whistling, a door slamming — felt like warnings she couldn't afford to ignore."
  e.g. "The intrusive image left her scanning every room she entered, cataloguing exits, tracking faces, unable to switch off."
  e.g. "Because the memory came back so vividly, she began to see threads of it everywhere: in strangers' faces, in certain times of day, in the quality of winter light."
